summary: A humorous April 1st RFC defining Concat notation, a text-based language for describing pictures and videos involving cats and containers. It is a joke, not a real specification.

subtitle: An April 1st notation describes cats, containers, and their positions in text.

tldr.problem: This April 1st RFC invents a compact text notation for describing pictures and videos of cats, containers, and interactions between them.
tldr.mechanism: Concat uses US-ASCII text, symbols for subjects and containers, operators for positions, and a state-change marker for changes over time.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides a formal grammar and examples for a playful subject. It is humorous and does not define a network protocol.

today: RFC 9402 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2023. It defines a humorous text notation for cat-related pictures and videos, not a network protocol.

sections.title: A Text Notation for Cat Media
sections.content: RFC 9402 defines Concat as a text-based language for describing pictures and videos whose subjects include cats, containers, and their interactions. It restricts its notation to US-ASCII characters so that the text can be transferred in environments with limited capabilities. The subject is treated in an intentionally formal style.
sections.plainLanguage: Concat is a way to describe cat pictures using text characters. This April 1st document gives the idea a formal grammar.

sections.title: Subjects, Containers, and Positions
sections.content: The word cat represents a cat; partial forms such as c, a, and t represent parts. Square brackets represent boxes, parentheses represent round containers, and curly braces represent soft containers. The plus sign marks horizontal placement, while a slash marks vertical placement.
sections.plainLanguage: Words identify subjects, brackets show containers, and symbols show position. For example, plus means side by side and slash means one above another.

sections.title: Repeated Objects and Changes Over Time
sections.content: The notation permits counts for repeated objects and uses => to mark significant changes in a video or animation. The RFC's examples include [cat] for a cat in a box, 3 * cat for three cats side by side, and cat1 + [cat2] => cat2 + [cat1] for two cats swapping places.
sections.plainLanguage: A number can show repeated subjects, and an arrow marks a change over time. One example shows two cats swapping places.
